evals.prompt: I need a function that formats a duration in milliseconds into a human-readable string like '2m 3s'. Where should this live? Should I make a new utils package for time formatting?
evals.expected_output: Walk the reuse-first ladder top-down before writing new code: (1) Does it need to exist? (2) Already in this repo — reuse a feature module, @pumni/* package export, hook, or helper; (3) platform/stdlib primitive (Intl.NumberFormat / Temporal / Date built-ins over hand-rolled); (4) already-installed dep; (5) is it a one-liner? Only then write the minimum new code. Do NOT create a new utils package for a single duration formatter — that is speculative abstraction for single-use code. Keep Web OS boundaries (RLS, server/client isolation, package graph) intact.
expectations: Walks the reuse-first ladder top-down before proposing new code (YAGNI, reuse repo helper/package export, prefer platform/stdlib primitive, installed dep, one-liner, then minimum new code)
Does not propose creating a new utils/package for a single duration formatter (rejects speculative abstraction for single-use code)
Prefers platform/stdlib built-ins (e.g. Intl) over a hand-rolled equivalent where applicable

evals.prompt: Let me extract an interface `IClient` and an `SupabaseClientAdapter` that wraps the Supabase client, so that in the future we could swap in a different backend. This makes the seam cleaner and more testable.
evals.expected_output: Reject introducing the IClient seam for a single adapter. One adapter is a hypothetical seam — two real variants make the seam credible. Do not introduce a seam just because it feels tidy. The existing request-scoped Supabase server client is already an acceptable seam; wrapping it in a one-adapter interface adds interface surface with no depth and no real second variant. Accept the dependency rather than constructing a hidden one-adapter abstraction unless a second real variant exists.
expectations: Rejects introducing the IClient interface for a single SupabaseClientAdapter (one adapter is a hypothetical seam)
States the rule: two real variants make the seam credible; one adapter is a hypothetical seam
Does not introduce a seam just because it feels tidy; prefers accepting the existing client dependency over constructing a hidden one-adapter abstraction
